issues.legal_issue: Processing an agriculturist’s own-grown produce does not remove the turnover exclusion when the processing is minimal and the produce retains its essential character.
material_facts: The seller was an agriculturist who owned tea gardens and grew the tea leaves on land in which he had an interest.
The leaves were withered, crushed, roasted, fermented under wet sheets, graded, and roasted again before sale.
The processing was undertaken to prevent the leaves from perishing, make them transportable and marketable, and bring out their flavour and colour.
The tea remained tea leaves in its essential substance and was sold as tea leaves; it was not transformed into a different commodity.
issues.conclusion: The processed tea leaves remained agricultural produce, so the sales were excluded from taxable turnover and were not exigible to sales tax. The appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(i) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, the proceeds from an agriculturist’s sale of agricultural produce grown by that person on land in which the person has an interest are excluded from turnover; section 3 charges tax on turnover. Agricultural produce does not lose that character merely because it undergoes processing needed to prevent deterioration or make it transportable and marketable. The test is whether the process is minimal in relation to the produce or so substantial that the produce would no longer be treated as agricultural produce in common parlance, in the market, or otherwise. The Court approved the approach in The State of Madras v. R. Saravana Pillai and the related arecanut decision in N. Deviah Gowder v. Commercial Tax Officer, and referred to decisions concerning other produce, including Deputy Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax and Sales Tax v. Sherneilly Rubber & Cardamom Estates Ltd. and Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P. v. Harbilas Rai and Sons. It distinguished Killing Valley Tea Company Ltd. v. Secretary to State, which concerned apportionment of agricultural and non-agricultural income, and distinguished The State of Madras v. Swasthik Tobacco Factory and The State of Madras v. Bell Mark Tobacco Co., where the goods sold were different from the raw material. It noted that the broader reasoning in R. B. N. S. Borawake v. The State of Bombay might require reconsideration, but did not need to rely on it for this decision.

predicates.sales_tax_exemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether sales by a producer are subject to sales tax or excluded from taxable turnover.
predicates.seller_grew_agricultural_produce_on_inte: The seller grew the agricultural produce on land in which the seller had an interest.
predicates.processing_was_minimal_and_for_marketabi: The seller processed the produce only to prevent deterioration or to make it transportable and marketable, and the processing was minimal in relation to that produce.
predicates.produce_retained_essential_character: After processing, the produce retained its essential character rather than becoming a different commodity.

issues.definition: When a sales-tax dispute concerns a seller’s own agricultural produce grown on land in which the seller has an interest, minimal processing for marketability that preserves the produce’s essential character results in the sale proceeds being excluded from taxable turnover.
